title: Yesterday, last week
topic: time expressions for the past; telling events in order
why: The words that place a story in time: yesterday, the day before yesterday, last week, a year ago, then, in the end. With them and the past tense of הָלַךְ, נָסַע and חָזַר, you can tell about a weekend from start to finish.

Placing a story in the past

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
אֶתְמוֹלetmolyesterday
אֶתְמוֹל בָּעֶרֶבetmol ba-erevlast night, yesterday evening
שִׁלְשׁוֹםshilshomthe day before yesterday
בְּסוֹף הַשָּׁבוּעַbe-sof ha-shavu'athis weekend, on the weekend
בַּשָּׁבוּעַ שֶׁעָבַרba-shavu'a she-avarlast week
בַּחֹדֶשׁ שֶׁעָבַרba-khodesh she-avarlast month
בַּשָּׁנָה שֶׁעָבְרָהba-shana she-avralast year

שֶׁעָבַר means \"that has passed\": it's the verb עָבַר (to pass) in the past tense! So it agrees with the noun: שָׁבוּעַ and חֹדֶשׁ are masculine → שֶׁעָבַר; שָׁנָה is feminine → שֶׁעָבְרָה. English \"last\" never changes, so this takes a little attention.

אֶתְמוֹל בָּעֶרֶב לָמַדְתִּי.Last night, I studied. [etmol ba-erev lamadti]

In Israel, the work week starts on Sunday: on Sunday morning at the office, everyone talks about their סוֹף שָׁבוּעַ (weekend, literally \"end of the week\").

", "

\"Ago\": לִפְנֵי comes first (and it isn't יֵשׁ!)

English puts \"ago\" after the amount of time; Hebrew puts לִפְנֵי (before) in front of it: \"a year ago\" is literally \"before a year.\" Don't reach for יֵשׁ (\"there is\") here: it has nothing to do with time.

לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה גַּרְתִּי בְּפָרִיז.A year ago, I lived in Paris. [lifnei shana garti be-Pariz]
הוּא חָזַר לִפְנֵי שָׁבוּעַ.He came back a week ago. [hu khazar lifnei shavu'a]
בָּאנוּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי שָׁלוֹשׁ שָׁנִים.We came to Israel three years ago. [banu le-Yisra'el lifnei shalosh shanim]

To tell things in order: קֹדֶם or בְּהַתְחָלָה (first, at the beginning), אַחַר כָּךְ (then, afterward), וְאָז (and then, so), בַּסּוֹף (in the end).

קֹדֶם אָכַלְנוּ, אַחַר כָּךְ הָלַכְנוּ לַיָּם, וּבַסּוֹף חָזַרְנוּ הַבַּיְתָה.First we ate, then we went to the sea, and in the end we went back home. [kodem akhalnu, akhar kakh halakhnu la-yam, u-va-sof khazarnu ha-bayta]

הַבַּיְתָה [ha-bayta] means \"toward home\": you use it with verbs of movement, without לְ, just like \"go home\" in English with no \"to.\" To be at home, it's always בַּבַּיִת.

", "

Going and coming back in the past

Good news: הוֹלֵךְ, נוֹסֵעַ, and חוֹזֵר (unit 7) are regular in the past, following the model of כָּתַב.

Pronounto go (on foot)to go (by vehicle)to come back, return
אֲנִיהָלַכְתִּי halakhtiנָסַעְתִּי nasatiחָזַרְתִּי khazarti
אַתָּההָלַכְתָּ halakhtaנָסַעְתָּ nasataחָזַרְתָּ khazarta
אַתְּהָלַכְתְּ halakhtנָסַעַתְּ nasa'atחָזַרְתְּ khazart
הוּאהָלַךְ halakhנָסַע nasaחָזַר khazar
הִיאהָלְכָה halkhaנָסְעָה nas'aחָזְרָה khazra
אֲנַחְנוּהָלַכְנוּ halakhnuנָסַעְנוּ nasanuחָזַרְנוּ khazarnu
אַתֶּםהֲלַכְתֶּם halakhtemנְסַעְתֶּם nesatemחֲזַרְתֶּם khazartem
אַתֶּןהֲלַכְתֶּן halakhtenנְסַעְתֶּן nesatenחֲזַרְתֶּן khazarten
הֵם / הֵןהָלְכוּ halkhuנָסְעוּ nas'uחָזְרוּ khazru

Remember: הָלַךְ on foot; נָסַע by bus, train, or car. For \"you\" (plural), the first vowel weakens, as in כְּתַבְתֶּם: הֲלַכְתֶּם, נְסַעְתֶּם, חֲזַרְתֶּם.

נָסַעַתְּ (you left, to a woman) takes an extra short a because of the final ע: [nasa'at]. In speech, many people just say [nasat].
